briefing.h: A war inside Spain, watched by the world
briefing.t: The Spanish Civil War began with a military coup against the elected government of the Second Republic on 17–18 July 1936 and ended with the unconditional victory of General Francisco Franco on 1 April 1939. The coup failed in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Bilbao and much of the industrial north and east, but succeeded in Spanish Morocco, the Canaries, most of the Balearics, Galicia, Old Castile, Navarre and pockets of western Andalusia. What was meant to be a quick seizure of power became a war of almost three years. It was at once a class war, a clash over religion and the Church, a struggle between centralism and regional autonomy (Catalonia, the Basque Country), and an early battleground of the wider European confrontation between fascism, communism and liberal democracy.

The Republican (loyalist) side was a coalition: the government of the Republic led in turn by José Giral, Francisco Largo Caballero and Juan Negrín; the left Republicans of President Manuel Azaña; the Socialists (PSOE) and their union UGT; the Communists (PCE), whose influence grew with Soviet aid; the anarcho-syndicalist CNT-FAI; the anti-Stalinist Marxist POUM; and the autonomous governments of Catalonia and the Basque Country. In summer 1936 party and union militias did most of the fighting; from late 1936 they were folded into the Ejército Popular (People's Army). Foreign volunteers of the International Brigades and Soviet tanks, aircraft and advisers — paid for with the Bank of Spain's gold reserve — were the Republic's main outside support. Mexico also sent arms.

The rebels called themselves nacionales; Republicans called them facciosos or rebeldes, and historians often use sublevados (the risen). Their core was the army, above all the professional Army of Africa — the Spanish Legion and Moroccan Regulares — commanded by Franco, with General Emilio Mola directing the plot from Pamplona. Civilian allies included the fascist Falange, the Carlist Requetés of Navarre, monarchists and much of the Catholic right (CEDA). In April 1937 Franco merged Falange and Carlists into a single party, FET y de las JONS. Nazi Germany sent the Condor Legion (air and armour, with rotating crews) and Fascist Italy the Corpo Truppe Volontarie (CTV) and the Aviazione Legionaria; Portugal gave logistic support and volunteers.

In the first summer rebel columns from the south advanced up the Tagus towards Madrid while Mola's northern forces fought for the Guadarrama passes. Madrid held in November 1936, and battles around it — Jarama, Guadalajara, Brunete — failed to break the stalemate. Franco turned north: Bilbao fell in June 1937, Santander in August and Asturias in October, giving the rebels the industrial north. Republican offensives at Belchite and Teruel won ground but could not keep it. In spring 1938 the Nationalists reached the Mediterranean at Vinaròs, cutting the Republic in two. The Republic's last great offensive, across the Ebro (July–November 1938), bled its army white. Catalonia fell in January–February 1939.

After Barcelona fell on 26 January 1939, around half a million people fled across the Pyrenees into France in the Retirada. Britain and France recognised Franco's government on 27 February and President Azaña resigned in exile. In the remaining central zone, Prime Minister Negrín wanted to resist in the hope that a European war would change the balance, but on 5 March Colonel Segismundo Casado seized power in Madrid to negotiate a surrender, leading to fighting among Republicans. Franco accepted only unconditional surrender. His troops entered Madrid on 28 March; thousands of Republicans waited in vain for ships at Alicante. Franco's final war communiqué was signed at Burgos on 1 April 1939. Formal war ended; repression, prison camps and exile did not.

The total death toll is still debated; a commonly cited overall figure is around half a million, but historians' estimates vary widely. Beyond combat deaths, both zones saw mass killing behind the lines. For the Nationalist zone during the war, estimates range from under 50,000 to 200,000 (Casanova c. 100,000; Thomas 75,000), with tens of thousands more executed after 1939. For the Republican zone, most historians place the figure around 38,000–55,000 (Beevor 38,000; Payne and Juliá 50,000; Thomas and Preston 55,000), including 6,832 clergy. Cities such as Madrid, Barcelona, Gernika, Valencia and Almería were bombed from the air. Hundreds of thousands went into exile; many never returned.

Under Franco (to 1975) only the victors' dead were honoured; the Valley of the Fallen (now Valle de Cuelgamuros) became the regime's great monument. The transition to democracy rested on an amnesty (1977) and an informal 'pact of forgetting'. From 2000 civil associations began exhuming mass graves. The Law of Historical Memory (Ley 52/2007, 26 December 2007) recognised victims of both sides, supported exhumations and ordered the removal of Francoist symbols. Franco's remains were moved from Cuelgamuros on 24 October 2019. The Democratic Memory Law (Ley 20/2022, in force 21 October 2022) replaced it: the state takes charge of exhumations and a DNA bank, Francoist court sentences are declared void, and the valley was renamed Cuelgamuros. The subject remains politically divisive, and several regions have their own memory laws.

Much of the war's landscape survives: trench lines in the Sierra de Guadarrama, Jarama and Aragon; ruined villages kept as memorials at Belchite and Corbera d'Ebre; bunkers of Bilbao's Iron Belt; air-raid shelters in Barcelona, Valencia, Cartagena and Almería; and mass-grave memorials in every region. Many sites are on open hillside or farmland — respect private land, do not dig or collect metal (it is illegal and unexploded ordnance is still found), and remember that many places are graves. This guide tries to present both sides' dead and both sides' crimes plainly and without glorification.

origins.t: After municipal elections in which Republican candidates swept the cities, King Alfonso XIII left Spain and the Second Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931. The new Cortes, dominated by Republicans and Socialists, passed a democratic constitution in December 1931 that separated Church and state, gave women the vote and allowed regional autonomy; Catalonia obtained its Statute in 1932. Under Prime Minister Manuel Azaña the government attempted army reform, agrarian reform in the great estates of the south, secular schooling and restrictions on the religious orders. The reforms raised huge hopes among landless labourers and workers, and deep alarm among landowners, much of the officer corps and Catholic Spain.

The Republic was attacked from right and left. In August 1932 General José Sanjurjo's coup attempt in Seville (the Sanjurjada) collapsed within a day. Anarchist insurrections broke out in 1932 and 1933; at Casas Viejas (Cádiz) in January 1933 Assault Guards killed villagers after a rising, damaging Azaña's government. The Catholic right organised in the mass party CEDA under José María Gil Robles, while José Antonio Primo de Rivera founded the Falange in October 1933. In the November 1933 elections — the first in which women voted — the centre-right won, and a Radical Party government under Alejandro Lerroux, dependent on CEDA votes, began to slow or reverse the reforms.

When three CEDA ministers entered the government in October 1934, the left called a revolutionary general strike. It failed in most of Spain, but in Catalonia President Lluís Companys proclaimed a 'Catalan State within a Spanish Federal Republic' on 6 October; it lasted about ten hours. In Asturias, miners of the UGT, CNT and Communists seized much of the region for two weeks (5–19 October). The government, with General Franco coordinating from Madrid, sent in the Legion and Moroccan Regulares. Hugh Thomas estimated about 2,000 deaths, including those killed in the repression, and 15,000–30,000 were arrested. Each side drew its own lesson: for the left, fascism was at the gates; for the right, revolution.

Scandals brought down the Radical-CEDA governments, and elections were called for 16 February 1936. The left united in the Popular Front (Republicans, Socialists, Communists, POUM, with anarchist voters largely turning out), against a right-wing coalition. The Popular Front won 267 seats to the right's 132 on a narrow popular-vote margin; the fairness of the count in some provinces is still argued over by historians (Villa García and Álvarez Tardío, 2017, versus their critics). Azaña formed a government, amnestied the 1934 prisoners and restored Catalan autonomy; in May he became President and Santiago Casares Quiroga Prime Minister. Land occupations, strikes, church burnings and street killings between left and right militants followed.

Army officers had begun conspiring soon after the election. The government moved suspect generals away from Madrid — Franco to the Canary Islands, Mola to Pamplona, Goded to the Balearics — which in practice let them build networks in the provinces. Mola, as 'the Director', drafted instructions calling for extreme violence to crush resistance. Sanjurjo, in exile in Portugal, was to lead the new regime. Monarchist and Carlist leaders pledged support; the Carlists offered thousands of armed Requetés in Navarre. The Falange, banned and its leader José Antonio imprisoned since March, joined the plot. Franco hesitated until late; a British-registered aircraft, the Dragon Rapide, was chartered in London to fly him from the Canaries to Morocco.

On 12 July 1936 gunmen of the right shot dead Lieutenant José Castillo of the Assault Guards, a known Socialist, in Madrid. In retaliation, in the early hours of 13 July a group of Assault Guards and Socialist militants seized the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo from his home and murdered him; his body was left at the East Cemetery. That men connected to the state's own police had killed a leading opposition deputy shocked conservative Spain and removed the last hesitations among some conspirators. Mola fixed the date of the rising for 17–18 July.

Warned that the plot had been discovered, the garrison in Melilla rose on the afternoon of 17 July; Ceuta and Tetuán followed and Spanish Morocco was in rebel hands by the next morning. On 18 July Franco proclaimed a state of war in Las Palmas and flew to Morocco; Queipo de Llano seized Seville; risings followed across the peninsula. Casares Quiroga refused to arm the unions and resigned; a compromise cabinet under Martínez Barrio lasted hours; on 19 July José Giral's government distributed arms to the workers' organisations. Where loyal Assault and Civil Guards joined armed workers — Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia — the coup failed. Where the army and Civil Guard held together, it succeeded. Spain was split in two.

people.name: Manuel Azaña
people.role: Prime Minister 1931–33 and 1936; President of the Republic 1936–39
people.t: A writer and left Republican intellectual, Azaña embodied the reforming Republic of 1931: army reform, secular education and Catalan autonomy. After the Popular Front victory he became Prime Minister, then President in May 1936. During the war he had little real power and grew pessimistic; his 1937 speech in Barcelona ended with the plea for 'peace, pity and pardon'. He crossed into France in the Retirada, resigned on 27 February 1939 after Britain and France recognised Franco, and died in exile at Montauban in November 1940.

people.name: Francisco Largo Caballero
people.role: UGT/PSOE leader; Prime Minister and War Minister Sep 1936–May 1937
people.t: A plasterer turned trade-union leader, head of the UGT and of the PSOE's left wing, nicknamed 'the Spanish Lenin' by admirers. He became Prime Minister on 4 September 1936 in a government that brought in Socialists, Communists and, from November, four anarchist ministers. He moved the government to Valencia in November 1936 and began building the Popular Army. Clashes with the Communists and the fallout of the Barcelona May Days forced him out in May 1937. In exile in France he was arrested and held in Sachsenhausen; he died in Paris in 1946.

people.name: Juan Negrín
people.role: Finance Minister 1936–37; Prime Minister May 1937–March 1939
people.t: A physiologist and Socialist, Negrín as Finance Minister organised the transfer of most of the Bank of Spain's gold reserve to Moscow in October–November 1936 to pay for Soviet arms — still a controversial decision. As Prime Minister from May 1937 he centralised the war effort, worked closely with the Communists and argued that 'to resist is to win', hoping that a general European war would save the Republic. His Thirteen Points (April 1938) set out peace terms. Ousted by Casado's coup in March 1939, he died in exile in Paris.

people.name: Dolores Ibárruri, 'La Pasionaria'
people.role: Communist deputy and PCE leader; orator
people.t: A miner's daughter from Gallarta (Biscay), Ibárruri became the best-known voice of the Spanish Communist Party. Her radio speech on 19 July 1936, ending '¡No pasarán!' ('They shall not pass'), became the slogan of the defence of Madrid. She toured fronts and rallies throughout the war and gave the farewell speech to the departing International Brigades in autumn 1938. She spent almost four decades in exile, mainly in the USSR, where her son died at Stalingrad, and returned to Spain in 1977, when she was again elected to the Cortes for Asturias.

people.name: Buenaventura Durruti
people.role: Anarchist (CNT-FAI) militant; leader of the Durruti Column
people.t: A metalworker from León and veteran anarchist activist, Durruti helped defeat the military rising in Barcelona in July 1936 and then led a militia column of several thousand onto the Aragon front, where collectivisation followed in its wake. In November 1936 he brought part of the column to Madrid and fought in the Ciudad Universitaria. He was mortally wounded near the Clinical Hospital on 19 November and died the next day. Whether he was hit by enemy fire, a stray shot or an accident is still disputed. Hundreds of thousands attended his funeral in Barcelona.

people.name: José Miaja
people.role: General; president of the Junta de Defensa de Madrid
people.t: An unremarkable career officer, Miaja was left in charge of Madrid when the government fled to Valencia on 6 November 1936, heading the Junta de Defensa with Vicente Rojo as chief of staff. The city held, and Miaja became a popular hero of the defence. He later commanded the Army of the Centre and took charge at Jarama. In March 1939 he backed Colonel Casado's council against Negrín, which led to the surrender of Madrid. He left for exile in Mexico and died there.

people.name: Vicente Rojo
people.role: Chief of staff of the Madrid defence, then of the Popular Army
people.t: A Catholic professional officer and staff-college teacher who stayed loyal to the Republic, Rojo organised the defence of Madrid in November 1936 and became chief of the central general staff in 1937. He planned the Republic's major offensives — Brunete, Belchite, Teruel and the Ebro — which achieved initial surprise but could not be sustained against Nationalist reserves and air power. He went into exile in Argentina and Bolivia, returned to Spain in 1957, was tried by a military court and sentenced, then pardoned, and died in Madrid.

people.name: Enrique Líster
people.role: Communist commander: 5th Regiment, 11th Division, V Army Corps
people.t: A Galician stonemason and Communist trained in Moscow, Líster rose from militia leader in the Communist 5th Regiment to one of the Popular Army's best-known commanders. His units fought at Madrid, Jarama, Guadalajara, Brunete and Teruel, where his division broke into the city in December 1937, and his V Corps led the Ebro crossing in July 1938. He was a hard disciplinarian, and his troops' dissolution of the anarchist Council of Aragon in August 1937 remains controversial. He lived in exile in the USSR and elsewhere, returning to Spain in 1977.

people.name: Juan Modesto
people.role: Communist commander of the Army of the Ebro
people.t: A former sawmill worker from Andalusia who had served as a corporal in the Legion, Modesto became a Communist militia leader in 1936 and rose through the Popular Army to command V Corps and then the Army of the Ebro in 1938. He directed the Republic's largest operation, the crossing of the Ebro on 25 July 1938, and the long defensive battle that followed. After the war he went into exile in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe and died in Prague in 1969.

people.name: Lluís Companys
people.role: President of the Generalitat de Catalunya 1934–40
people.t: A lawyer and leader of Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya, Companys proclaimed a Catalan State in October 1934 and was imprisoned until 1936. When the coup failed in Barcelona he met the victorious anarchists and accepted their Central Committee of Anti-Fascist Militias alongside the Generalitat. Tensions with the central government and between anarchists and Communists culminated in the May Days of 1937. He fled to France in 1939, was arrested by the Gestapo in 1940, handed to Franco and shot at Montjuïc castle on 15 October 1940.

people.name: José Antonio Aguirre
people.role: First Lehendakari (President) of the Basque Government
people.t: A Catholic lawyer and leader of the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV), Aguirre was sworn in beneath the oak of Gernika on 7 October 1936, after the Cortes passed the Basque Statute. His government ran Biscay as a largely autonomous state, organised its own army (Eusko Gudarostea) and protected the Church. After the fall of Bilbao in June 1937 Basque units surrendered to the Italians at Santoña in August under an agreement that was not honoured. Aguirre led the Basque government in exile until his death in Paris in 1960.

people.name: Federico García Lorca
people.role: Poet and playwright; killed by the rebels
people.t: Spain's most celebrated poet and dramatist of the period, Lorca was a Republican sympathiser but not a party activist. He was in Granada when the city fell to the rebels in July 1936. Arrested at the house of the Falangist Rosales family, he was taken to Víznar and shot in the ravine between Víznar and Alfacar around 18 August 1936, alongside a schoolteacher and two anarchist banderilleros. His remains have never been found despite several searches. His killing became a symbol of the repression in the Nationalist zone.

people.name: Francisco Franco
people.role: Commander of the Army of Africa; Generalísimo and Head of State
people.t: Spain's youngest general, a veteran of the Moroccan wars and co-founder of the Legion, Franco was posted to the Canaries in 1936 and joined the plot late. Flown to Morocco on 19 July, he secured German and Italian aircraft to ferry the Army of Africa to the mainland. On 1 October 1936 he became Generalísimo and Head of State, directing the war from Salamanca and Burgos with methodical, attritional caution. He ruled as dictator until his death in 1975. He was buried at Cuelgamuros; his remains were moved to Mingorrubio cemetery in 2019.

people.name: Emilio Mola
people.role: 'The Director' of the 1936 plot; commander of the Army of the North
people.t: Military governor of Pamplona, Mola organised the conspiracy under the codename 'the Director' and secured the support of the Carlists. His instructions called for extreme violence against opponents. When the coup failed to take Madrid, his northern columns were stopped in the Guadarrama passes. He commanded the 1937 campaign against the Basque Country, including the bombing of Durango and Gernika. He was killed when his aircraft crashed near Alcocero (Burgos) on 3 June 1937; the village was renamed Alcocero de Mola.

people.name: Gonzalo Queipo de Llano
people.role: General; leader of the rising in Seville and ruler of western Andalusia
people.t: A general once seen as a Republican, Queipo seized Seville on 18 July 1936 with a small force, bluff and ruthlessness. From Radio Sevilla he broadcast nightly speeches mixing propaganda, threats and crude sexual intimidation of Republican women. Western Andalusia under his command saw one of the war's harshest repressions, with many thousands shot. He led the southern army that took Málaga in February 1937. Buried in the Basilica of La Macarena, his remains were removed in November 2022 under the Democratic Memory Law.

people.name: Juan Yagüe
people.role: Commander of the Army of Africa columns; later Moroccan Corps
people.t: A Falange-sympathising Legion officer who had fought in Asturias in 1934, Yagüe led the Army of Africa columns north from Seville in August 1936 through Mérida and Badajoz, where hundreds or thousands of prisoners were shot after the city's capture (numbers disputed). He told an American journalist that of course they had shot them. Relieved at Toledo, he returned to command the Moroccan Army Corps in Aragon in 1938 and on the Ebro. He was Air Minister in 1939–40.

people.name: José Enrique Varela
people.role: General; Madrid assault and Teruel counter-offensive
people.t: A twice-decorated veteran of Morocco (Laureate Cross) with Carlist sympathies, Varela secured Cádiz for the rebels in July 1936, then led the columns that relieved the Alcázar of Toledo on 27 September and attacked Madrid in November 1936. He commanded at Jarama in February 1937 and led one of the corps that retook Teruel in 1938. As Army Minister after the war he clashed with the Falange.

people.name: José Moscardó
people.role: Colonel; commander of the Alcázar of Toledo during the siege
people.t: Military governor of Toledo, Moscardó held the Alcázar fortress with about a thousand Civil Guards, soldiers, Falangists and their families, plus civilian hostages, from 21 July to 27 September 1936. The best-known story — a telephone call in which he told his captured son Luis to die bravely — became a pillar of Francoist legend; Luis was shot weeks later, though the details of the call have been questioned. Relieved by Varela, Moscardó became a Nationalist hero and later a general.

people.name: José Antonio Primo de Rivera
people.role: Founder and leader of the Falange
people.t: Son of the 1920s dictator Miguel Primo de Rivera, José Antonio founded the fascist Falange Española in 1933. Arrested in March 1936, he was in prison in Alicante when the war began. A Republican court tried him for conspiracy and he was shot on 20 November 1936 — the same day Durruti died. The Franco regime turned him into a martyr ('el Ausente'); his remains were moved to the Valley of the Fallen in 1959 and exhumed in April 2023 for reburial in a Madrid cemetery.

people.name: Wolfram von Richthofen
people.role: Chief of staff, then commander of the German Condor Legion
people.t: A First World War pilot and engineer, and cousin of the 'Red Baron', Richthofen served as the Condor Legion's chief of staff from January 1937 and developed close air support tactics with the Nationalist army in the Basque campaign. He was in charge of air operations when Gernika was bombed on 26 April 1937. He commanded the Legion from late 1938 to the end of the war. In the Second World War he became a Luftwaffe field marshal; he died in 1945.

people.name: Mario Roatta
people.role: Commander of the Italian Corpo Truppe Volontarie (CTV)
people.t: An Italian general and former head of military intelligence, Roatta led Italian troops in the rapid capture of Málaga in February 1937. A month later his motorised CTV divisions attacked towards Guadalajara, but mud, Republican air power, Soviet tanks and a counter-attack in which Italian anti-fascists fought against them turned the battle into a defeat widely publicised as a humiliation for Mussolini. He was replaced and later served as army chief of staff; he was accused of war crimes in Yugoslavia.

people.name: The International Brigades
people.role: Foreign volunteers in the Republican army, 1936–38
people.t: Recruited largely through Communist parties and based at Albacete, volunteers from dozens of countries formed the XI to XV Brigades and others. Estimates of total numbers vary, commonly around 32,000–35,000, with some counts higher. They fought at Madrid, Jarama, Guadalajara, Brunete, Belchite, Teruel and the Ebro, often as shock troops, with heavy losses. Discipline could be harsh and political control strict. They were withdrawn in autumn 1938 and paraded through Barcelona on 28 October 1938.

people.name: George Orwell
people.role: British writer; militiaman with the POUM
people.t: Eric Blair came to Barcelona in December 1936 and joined the militia of the POUM, serving on the quiet Aragon front in the Sierra de Alcubierre and near Huesca. On leave in Barcelona he witnessed the May Days of 1937. Back at the front he was shot through the throat on 20 May 1937. When the POUM was outlawed and its leaders arrested, he escaped to France. His account, Homage to Catalonia (1938), is one of the classic books on the war.

people.name: Norman Bethune
people.role: Canadian surgeon; mobile blood-transfusion pioneer
people.t: A Canadian thoracic surgeon and Communist, Bethune set up a mobile blood-transfusion service in Madrid in late 1936, bringing stored blood to front-line casualties. In February 1937 he and his team drove along the Málaga–Almería road ferrying refugees fleeing the fall of Málaga and documented the attacks on them. He left Spain in 1937, went to China to serve with the Communist Eighth Route Army, and died there of blood poisoning in 1939.

people.name: Ernest Hemingway
people.role: American writer and war correspondent
people.t: Hemingway reported the war for the North American Newspaper Alliance in 1937–38, staying at the Hotel Florida in besieged Madrid and visiting the Jarama, Guadalajara, Teruel and Ebro fronts. He helped make the documentary The Spanish Earth (1937) with Joris Ivens and wrote the play The Fifth Column. His novel For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), set among guerrillas in the Sierra de Guadarrama, shaped how English-speaking readers imagined the war.

people.name: Robert Capa and Gerda Taro
people.role: Photojournalists
people.t: Hungarian-born Endre Friedmann and German-born Gerta Pohorylle created the 'Robert Capa' name together in Paris. Their photographs from the Republican zone set the standard for modern war photography. Capa's 'Falling Soldier' (September 1936, Córdoba front) is famous and much debated over whether it was staged and where it was taken. Taro was fatally injured on 25 July 1937 when a tank struck the car she was riding on near Brunete, and died the next day. Capa was killed in Indochina in 1954.

time.title: Rising in Melilla
time.t: Warned that the plot had been uncovered, officers in Melilla rise on the afternoon of 17 July, a day early. Ceuta and Tetuán follow overnight; loyal officers and trade unionists are shot. Spanish Morocco, base of the Army of Africa, is secured for the rebels.

time.title: Queipo de Llano takes Seville
time.t: Queipo de Llano arrests the divisional commander around midday and, with a few hundred troops and bluff, seizes the centre of Seville. The civil governor surrenders that evening; working-class districts such as Triana resist until 20–22 July, when they are crushed with Legion reinforcements.

time.title: Coup defeated in Barcelona
time.t: Troops leave their barracks before dawn but are fought to a standstill by CNT militants, Assault Guards and, decisively, the Civil Guard. General Goded, flown in from Mallorca, is captured and broadcasts an appeal to stop fighting. The last rebel barracks surrender on 20 July.

time.title: Mola declares war in Pamplona
time.t: General Mola proclaims a state of war in Navarre, where thousands of Carlist Requetés in red berets mobilise alongside the army and Falangists. Within days columns leave Pamplona for the Guadarrama passes, Aragon and Gipuzkoa, and killings of Republican supporters begin across the province.

time.title: Storming of the Cuartel de la Montaña
time.t: Militias, Assault Guards and loyal troops besiege and storm the Montaña barracks in Madrid, where General Fanjul had gathered rebel officers and Falangists. Many defenders are killed after the surrender. The coup in Madrid collapses. The Temple of Debod now stands on the site.

time.title: Airlift across the Strait
time.t: From 19–20 July Army of Africa troops are flown to Seville, from early August in German Ju 52s and Italian SM.81s — the first large military airlift. A sea convoy crosses on 5 August despite the Republican navy.

time.title: Fighting for the Guadarrama passes
time.t: Mola's columns and Republican militias from Madrid fight for the Alto del León and Somosierra passes. The rebels hold the passes but cannot break through; the Sierra becomes a static front for the rest of the war.

time.title: Fall of Badajoz
time.t: Yagüe's Legion and Regulares storm Badajoz, linking the southern and northern rebel zones. Mass executions follow, many reportedly in the bullring. Estimates range from several hundred to around 4,000; Francisco Espinosa documented 1,341 names as a minimum.

time.title: Republican landing on Mallorca
time.t: Captain Alberto Bayo lands several thousand Catalan and Valencian militiamen near Porto Cristo and Sa Coma. Italian aircraft and reinforcements support the defenders, the bridgehead stalls, and the expedition is withdrawn on 3–4 September. Mallorca stays Nationalist and becomes an Italian air base for raids on the coast.

time.title: Killing of Federico García Lorca
time.t: Spain's best-known poet is shot by rebel-side forces in the ravine between Víznar and Alfacar, near Granada, one of thousands killed in Granada province in the first months of the war. The exact date and place of burial remain unknown; several searches have found nothing.

time.title: Largo Caballero government
time.t: Francisco Largo Caballero, leader of the UGT, forms a government of Socialists, Republicans and Communists, joined by Basque and Catalan ministers and, in November, four CNT anarchists. It begins turning the party and union militias into a regular Popular Army with mixed brigades and political commissars.

time.title: Irun and San Sebastián fall
time.t: Mola's columns, with Carlist volunteers and air support, take Irun on 5 September after fierce fighting; parts of the town are burned by its retreating defenders. The northern Republican zone loses its land border with France. San Sebastián is occupied without a battle on 13 September.

time.title: Relief of the Alcázar of Toledo
time.t: After a siege of about 70 days, Varela's columns relieve Moscardó's garrison in the ruined Alcázar; killings of militiamen and wounded in the city follow. Franco's decision to divert to Toledo boosted his prestige at home and abroad but gave Madrid time to prepare its defence.

time.title: Franco becomes Generalísimo and Head of State
time.t: Meeting near Salamanca in late September, the rebel generals name Franco supreme military commander; the decree also makes him head of the 'Government of the Spanish State'. He is formally invested in Burgos on 1 October 1936 and rules the Nationalist zone as a personal dictatorship from then on.

time.title: Basque government sworn in at Gernika
time.t: Days after the Cortes approves the Basque Statute of Autonomy, José Antonio Aguirre of the PNV takes the oath as first Lehendakari under the Tree of Gernika. His government, a coalition of Basque nationalists and the Popular Front parties, runs Biscay until June 1937.

time.title: Siege of Oviedo relieved
time.t: Colonel Aranda's garrison, which declared for the rebels on 19 July and was besieged by Asturian miners' militias through the summer and autumn, is relieved by a column from Galicia. Oviedo remains a narrow Nationalist salient under constant fire until Asturias falls in October 1937.

time.title: Gold leaves Cartagena for Moscow
time.t: Most of the Bank of Spain's gold reserve is shipped from Cartagena to the USSR as payment for arms. The Soviet tanks and aircraft appearing at Madrid that autumn are the first return.

time.title: Government leaves Madrid
time.t: With rebel columns at the south-western edge of the city, the Largo Caballero government leaves for Valencia on the night of 6 November, leaving General Miaja and a Junta de Defensa to hold Madrid. Many saw it as flight; the city's defence became a popular cause worldwide.

time.title: Paracuellos killings
time.t: Prisoners taken from Madrid jails in 'sacas' are shot at Paracuellos del Jarama and Torrejón. Many historians put the dead at around 2,000–3,000, though claims range much higher. Responsibility — the Junta's public-order officials including Santiago Carrillo, Communist cadres, Soviet advisers, militias — is disputed.

time.title: Assault on Madrid
time.t: Varela's columns attack through the Casa de Campo and Carabanchel. The XI International Brigade arrives the same day. Fighting spreads into the Ciudad Universitaria from 15 November, where Durruti is mortally wounded on 19 November. By 23 November Franco abandons the frontal assault.
time.place: Madrid, Casa de Campo / Ciudad Universitaria

time.title: José Antonio executed in Alicante
time.t: José Antonio Primo de Rivera, founder of the Falange, imprisoned since before the war, is tried for conspiracy and military rebellion by a Republican people's court and shot in Alicante prison. The Nationalist zone kept his death officially quiet for some time; later he became the regime's great martyr.

time.title: Lopera
time.t: A Republican attack on the Córdoba front near Lopera, including the XIV International Brigade and its British company, fails against Nationalist positions with heavy losses. The young British poet John Cornford and the writer Ralph Fox are among the volunteers killed around this time.

time.title: Battle of Jarama
time.t: Nationalists cross the Jarama to cut the Madrid–Valencia road. The XV International Brigade, including British and American volunteers, suffers heavy losses at 'Suicide Hill' and Pingarrón. The road stays open.

time.title: Fall of Málaga and the 'Desbandá'
time.t: Nationalist and Italian forces take Málaga on 8 February. Tens of thousands flee along the coast road to Almería and are shelled from the sea and attacked from the air. Deaths are uncertain; about 3,000 is often cited. Mass executions follow in Málaga.

time.title: Battle of Guadalajara
time.t: Italian CTV motorised divisions advance down the Zaragoza road, are stopped in rain and mud and routed by a Republican counter-attack around Brihuega, with Italian anti-fascists of the Garibaldi Battalion on the Republican side.

time.title: Bombing of Durango
time.t: Italian and Nationalist aircraft bomb Durango as Mola's offensive against Biscay opens, killing some 250 or more civilians (estimates vary), including a priest and worshippers at Mass in churches. The raid, four weeks before Gernika, marked a new stage in the bombing of undefended towns.

time.title: Unification decree
time.t: In Salamanca Franco merges the fascist Falange and the Carlist Comunión Tradicionalista into one party, FET y de las JONS, under his own leadership. Falangist leader Manuel Hedilla, who resisted, is arrested and sentenced to death, later commuted. All other parties in the Nationalist zone are dissolved.

time.title: Bombing of Gernika
time.t: Condor Legion and Italian bombers attack Gernika on a market Monday, 16:30–19:30. The Basque government reported 1,654 dead; modern research gives about 150–300. Picasso's painting makes it the emblem of the bombing of civilians.

time.title: Fall of Santa María de la Cabeza
time.t: Civil Guards, their families and right-wing civilians, about 1,200 people, besieged since September 1936 in the mountain sanctuary near Andújar, surrender after a final Republican assault. Their commander, Captain Santiago Cortés, dies of his wounds. The siege became a Nationalist legend like the Alcázar.
time.place: Santuario de la Virgen de la Cabeza

time.title: May Days in Barcelona
time.t: Fighting breaks out when Assault Guards try to take the CNT-held Telefónica. Anarchists and the POUM fight Communists and the government's police. Several hundred die; the POUM is then suppressed and its leader Andreu Nin murdered.

time.title: Death of Mola
time.t: General Mola, commander of the Army of the North and architect of the 1936 plot, is killed when his aircraft crashes in bad weather near Alcocero, north of Burgos, during the Biscay campaign. Franco's position as sole leader is strengthened. The village was renamed Alcocero de Mola.

time.title: Fall of Bilbao
time.t: After an engineer who knew its plans defected and the Iron Belt was breached at its weakest point on 12 June, Basque forces withdraw westward. Nationalist troops enter Bilbao on 19 June without large-scale destruction, as Basque units had prevented the demolition of factories and bridges.

time.title: Battle of Brunete
time.t: The Popular Army's first big offensive west of Madrid takes Brunete but stalls in extreme heat against Nationalist reserves and German aircraft. Losses are heavy on both sides; Gerda Taro is killed.

time.title: Belchite
time.t: The Republican offensive towards Zaragoza takes Quinto and Codo, then the fortified town of Belchite after two weeks of house-to-house fighting in summer heat. Zaragoza is never reached and the northern campaign is not diverted. The ruined old town is later left standing as a war memorial.

time.title: Fall of Santander
time.t: Nationalist and Italian forces take Santander after a rapid offensive. Basque units that had retreated into Cantabria surrender to the Italian CTV at Santoña under an agreement meant to guarantee their lives; Franco did not honour it, and many were imprisoned or executed.

time.title: Fall of Gijón
time.t: Nationalist columns enter Gijón, ending the war in the North and giving Franco its coal, steel and arms industries. Thousands of Asturian soldiers and militants take to the mountains, where some keep up guerrilla resistance for years; many others are killed or imprisoned.

time.title: Government moves to Barcelona
time.t: Negrín's government leaves Valencia for Barcelona, joining the President and aiming to put the Catalan war industry under central control. Relations with the Generalitat of Companys become strained as Catalan autonomy is steadily reduced during the last year and a half of the war.

time.title: Republicans attack Teruel
time.t: In snow and bitter cold, without preliminary bombardment, the Popular Army encircles Teruel and fights its way into the town. Colonel Rey d'Harcourt's garrison holds out in the Seminary, the Bank of Spain and other buildings until it surrenders on 8 January 1938.

time.title: Alfambra breakthrough
time.t: A Nationalist offensive north of Teruel, spearheaded by Monasterio's cavalry division in one of the last large cavalry charges in European warfare, breaks the Republican front along the Alfambra river and takes thousands of prisoners. The collapse leaves Teruel open to encirclement.

time.title: Nationalists retake Teruel
time.t: Almost encircled, Republican forces withdraw south along the Turia and Teruel, reduced to ruins, returns to Nationalist hands. Losses on both sides in the two-month battle were enormous, with many cases of frostbite; the Popular Army's reserves are spent.

time.title: Aragon offensive begins
time.t: A massive Nationalist offensive with strong air and armoured support breaks through the Republican front south of the Ebro, weakened by losses at Teruel. Belchite is retaken on 10 March, Caspe soon after; International Brigade units are shattered in the retreat, and the advance rolls towards Catalonia and the sea.

time.title: Bombing of Barcelona
time.t: Italian bombers of the Aviazione Legionaria flying from Mallorca attack Barcelona in waves every few hours for three days, 16–18 March. Between 1,000 and 1,300 civilians are killed and at least 2,000 wounded. International protests follow; the city's network of shelters expands.

time.title: Fall of Lleida
time.t: Nationalist troops take Lleida after street fighting in which El Campesino's division defends the city; the front in Catalonia settles along the Segre river. Catalonia's hydroelectric plants in the Pyrenees are soon lost, adding to the Republic's industrial difficulties.

time.title: Nationalists reach the sea at Vinaròs
time.t: Navarrese troops under Camilo Alonso Vega reach the Mediterranean coast at Vinaròs on Good Friday, 15 April. The Republican zone is cut in two: Catalonia in the north, and the larger centre-south zone with Madrid and Valencia. Many expected the war to end within weeks.

time.title: Fall of Castellón
time.t: Franco turns south towards Valencia rather than into Catalonia. Castellón falls on 14 June, but the advance is halted in July in front of the XYZ Line, a deep network of trenches and bunkers in the mountains north of Valencia, at heavy cost to the attackers.

time.title: Crossing of the Ebro
time.t: Shortly after midnight the Army of the Ebro crosses the river by boats, footbridges and pontoons at a dozen points between Mequinenza and Miravet, with a diversion at Amposta. It advances up to 20 km in a few days, reaching the outskirts of Gandesa.

time.title: Pàndols and Cavalls
time.t: Successive Nationalist counter-offensives, supported by overwhelming air and artillery superiority, grind against Republican positions on the bare rocky ridges of the Serra de Pàndols and Serra de Cavalls. Losses on both sides are among the heaviest of the war.

time.title: Farewell to the International Brigades
time.t: Withdrawn under a Non-Intervention scheme announced by Negrín at the League of Nations, the International Brigades parade through Barcelona before cheering crowds. Many volunteers from dictatorships have no home to go to; some later rejoin the fighting in the final weeks.

time.title: End of the Battle of the Ebro
time.t: The last Republican troops recross the Ebro at Flix on 16 November after a final Nationalist breakthrough in the Serra de Cavalls. Estimated casualties range from 50,000 to over 100,000; the Republic's best army is broken and Catalonia lies open.

time.title: Catalonia offensive
time.t: Nationalist armies with strong Italian participation attack along the Segre and Ebro fronts on 23 December. The exhausted Republican defence collapses in stages; Tarragona falls on 15 January 1939, and columns converge on Barcelona while refugees crowd the roads north.

time.title: Fall of Barcelona
time.t: Nationalist troops enter Barcelona almost without resistance, the government having left for Girona and Figueres. Tens of thousands of civilians and soldiers are already heading for the French border; arrests and courts-martial follow in the city.

time.title: The Retirada
time.t: Nearly half a million refugees and soldiers cross into France via La Jonquera, Portbou and mountain passes and are held in camps such as Argelès. Nationalist troops reach the border on 10 February.

time.title: Last Cortes at Figueres
time.t: The Republican Cortes meets for the last time on Spanish soil in the cellars of the castle of Sant Ferran at Figueres. Negrín sets out minimum conditions for peace — independence, free choice of government by the Spanish people, and no reprisals — which Franco ignores.

time.title: Casado's coup
time.t: Colonel Segismundo Casado, with Socialist Julián Besteiro and anarchist support, forms a National Defence Council in Madrid against Negrín's government, hoping to negotiate terms. Fighting with Communist units follows in Madrid. In Cartagena a rising leads the Republican fleet to sail for Bizerte.

time.title: Madrid surrenders
time.t: Nationalist troops enter Madrid. At Alicante the British ship Stanbrook sails with some 2,600 refugees; thousands more left on the quay are interned, many in the Campo de los Almendros.

time.title: Last war communiqué
time.t: Franco signs the final war communiqué at the Palacio de la Isla in Burgos: the Red Army captured and disarmed, 'the war has ended'. The USA recognises his government the same day. Repression, prison camps and executions continue for years.

time.title: Valley of the Fallen built
time.t: The basilica and giant cross at Cuelgamuros are built from 1940, partly with the labour of political prisoners, and inaugurated in 1959. Remains of over 33,000 dead from both sides are moved there, many Republicans without their families' consent; exhumations for identification began in 2023.

time.title: Law of Historical Memory
time.t: Ley 52/2007, passed under Prime Minister Rodríguez Zapatero, recognises victims of persecution and violence on both sides, supports the location and exhumation of mass graves, and orders the removal of Francoist symbols from public buildings and streets. Critics on the right saw it as reopening old wounds.

time.title: Franco exhumed
time.t: After a long legal battle with his family, Franco's remains are removed from the basilica at Cuelgamuros by helicopter and reburied beside his wife in the Mingorrubio cemetery at El Pardo, north of Madrid. The move was widely seen as a milestone in Spain's reckoning with the dictatorship.

time.title: Democratic Memory Law in force
time.t: Ley 20/2022 replaces the 2007 law. It makes the state responsible for searching for and exhuming the disappeared, creates a DNA bank, declares Francoist court sentences void, dissolves the Franco foundation and renames the valley Cuelgamuros. It remains politically contested.

factors.t: Fearing a general European war, Britain and France sponsored a Non-Intervention Agreement in August 1936, overseen by a committee in London from September. Germany, Italy and the USSR signed it and broke it. In practice it denied the legal government of Spain the right to buy arms openly, while Germany and Italy supplied the rebels on a large scale. France closed its border for much of the war. Historians broadly agree that non-intervention worked against the Republic, which was pushed into dependence on the Soviet Union.

The rebels received German aircraft, tanks, artillery and the Condor Legion (about 16,000 Germans served over time), and Italian troops, aircraft and arms on a larger scale (Italy's CTV numbered up to about 50,000 at a time), with Portuguese help and volunteers. The Republic's main supplier was the USSR, which sent aircraft, T-26 tanks, artillery and some 3,000 advisers and technicians, paid for with Spain's gold reserve; Mexico sent rifles. International Brigade volunteers added tens of thousands of fighters. Axis aid was steadier and was easier to deliver than Soviet shipments across the Mediterranean.

factors.h: The Army of Africa and the airlift
factors.t: The rebels' best troops — the Legion and the Moroccan Regulares — were stranded in Morocco when the Republican fleet, whose crews had largely mutinied against their officers, blocked the Strait. From late July 1936 German Junkers Ju 52s and Italian Savoia-Marchetti SM.81s flew thousands of men to Seville, the first large-scale military airlift. These professional soldiers drove north through Extremadura to the outskirts of Madrid in three months, defeating militias in open country and carrying out mass killings along the way.

The Republic combined a liberal-democratic government with a social revolution that broke out in July 1936 in Catalonia, Aragon and elsewhere: collectivised land and factories, militia rule and anticlerical violence. Anarchists and the POUM wanted to push the revolution forward; Communists, Socialists and Republicans wanted a centralised state and army first. The conflict erupted in the Barcelona May Days of 1937 and ended in the suppression of the POUM, and again in Casado's coup against Negrín in March 1939. The Nationalists, by contrast, were unified under one command and one party from 1937.

factors.h: Air power and the bombing of cities
factors.t: Spain was a testing ground for air war. German and Italian aircraft, and in 1936–37 Soviet fighters and bombers on the Republican side, fought for air superiority, which the Nationalists held from 1938. Madrid was bombed and shelled from November 1936; Durango and Gernika were destroyed in 1937; Italian aircraft from Mallorca raided Barcelona, Valencia, Alicante and other coastal cities. Republican aircraft also bombed Nationalist-held cities such as Córdoba, Valladolid and Palma. The response — hundreds of public air-raid shelters built by municipalities and neighbours — is one of the war's most visitable legacies.

factors.h: Holding Madrid and the problem of logistics
factors.t: The failure to take Madrid in November 1936 turned a coup into a long war. Soviet tanks and aircraft, the International Brigades, a disciplined Communist-led militia and the city's mass mobilisation stopped the assault; the Nationalists dug in at the Ciudad Universitaria and Casa de Campo for over two years. The Republic's offensives from 1937 won surprise but failed on supply, reserves and command: it could not replace equipment losses, while the Nationalists held the food-producing interior, the northern industry after 1937, and steadier foreign supply.

Both zones saw mass killing of perceived enemies, especially in the first months: in the Republican zone clergy, landowners, right-wing politicians and suspected rebels; in the Nationalist zone left-wing activists, trade unionists, officials and teachers, often through systematic military orders. After victory the Franco regime continued executions, camps and prison labour for years. Refugee flows marked the war: the Desbandá from Málaga in 1937, and the Retirada of nearly half a million people into France in 1939. Many exiles stayed in France, Mexico, the USSR and Latin America; some ended up in Nazi camps.

clock: Warned that their plans had been discovered, officers in Melilla rise early, seize the garrison and arrest the loyal commander, General Romerales.
The rising spreads to Ceuta and Tetuán; loyal officers and trade unionists are shot. Spanish Morocco is in rebel hands by the next morning.
Franco goes to the military headquarters in Las Palmas and proclaims a state of war; his manifesto is broadcast.
The government in Madrid announces that the rising is limited to Morocco. Prime Minister Casares Quiroga refuses to arm the UGT and CNT.
Queipo de Llano enters divisional HQ in Seville and arrests General Villa-Abrille.
The Dragon Rapide takes off from Gando with Franco aboard, bound for Morocco via Agadir and Casablanca.
Seville's civil governor surrenders to Queipo, who broadcasts on Radio Sevilla that night. Risings also in Cádiz and Córdoba.
Casares Quiroga resigns. Diego Martínez Barrio tries to form a compromise cabinet; Mola refuses by telephone.
Troops leave barracks in Barcelona and are met by CNT militants, Assault Guards and later the Civil Guard.
Mola proclaims a state of war in Pamplona; Carlist Requetés mobilise.
Franco lands at Tetuán and takes command of the Army of Africa.
José Giral forms a government that dissolves rebel units and hands arms to the workers' organisations.
Goded, who flew in from Mallorca around midday, is captured and broadcasts an appeal to lay down arms. The first Army of Africa troops are flown to Seville.
Militias and loyal forces storm the Cuartel de la Montaña in Madrid; Atarazanas barracks in Barcelona surrenders. Sanjurjo is killed in a plane crash at Estoril. Spain is divided.
glossary: CNT
Confederación Nacional del Trabajo — the anarcho-syndicalist trade union, strongest in Catalonia, Aragon and Andalusia.
FAI
Federación Anarquista Ibérica — the militant anarchist federation closely linked to the CNT (CNT-FAI).
UGT
Unión General de Trabajadores — the Socialist trade union, led by Largo Caballero.
PSOE
Partido Socialista Obrero Español — the Socialist Party, divided between moderates (Prieto) and a revolutionary left (Largo Caballero).
PCE
Partido Comunista de España — small in 1936, it grew rapidly during the war thanks to Soviet aid and its discipline.
PSUC
Partit Socialista Unificat de Catalunya — the Catalan Communist-aligned party formed in July 1936.
POUM
Partido Obrero de Unificación Marxista — anti-Stalinist Marxist party, strongest in Catalonia; suppressed after May 1937. Orwell served in its militia.
ERC
Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya — Catalan left-republican party of Companys.
PNV
Partido Nacionalista Vasco — the Catholic Basque Nationalist Party of Aguirre.
CEDA
Confederación Española de Derechas Autónomas — the mass Catholic right-wing party of Gil Robles.
Falange
Falange Española (de las JONS) — the fascist party founded by José Antonio Primo de Rivera in 1933; its militia grew hugely after July 1936.
FET y de las JONS
The single party created by Franco's unification decree of April 1937, merging Falangists and Carlists.
Carlists
Traditionalist monarchists, strongest in Navarre, loyal to a rival branch of the Bourbons; fervently Catholic.
Requetés
The Carlist militia, recognisable by their red berets; a key rebel force in 1936.
Regulares
Moroccan infantry and cavalry units of the Spanish army under Spanish officers, part of the Army of Africa.
Legión
The Spanish Foreign Legion (Tercio), shock troops of the Army of Africa, co-founded by Millán-Astray and Franco.
Guardia Civil
The rural paramilitary police; it split in 1936, and its choice often decided who won a town.
Guardia de Asalto
The Republic's urban Assault Guard, created in 1931; mostly loyal in July 1936.
Checa
Unofficial detention and interrogation centre run by parties, unions or police in the Republican zone, especially in 1936.
Paseo
'Taking for a ride' — extra-judicial killing of a detainee, usually at night on a roadside or cemetery wall, in both zones in 1936.
Saca
The removal of prisoners from a jail to be killed, as at Paracuellos in 1936 and in Nationalist-zone jails.
Brigadas Internacionales
The International Brigades of foreign volunteers in the Republican army, 1936–38.
Legión Cóndor
The German air and ground unit sent by Hitler to support Franco, 1936–39.
CTV
Corpo Truppe Volontarie — Mussolini's expeditionary corps of Italian troops in Spain.
Ejército Popular
The Republic's Popular Army, formed from late 1936 from the militias and loyal units, organised in mixed brigades.
Sublevados
'Those who rose' — neutral term for the rebels of July 1936.
Nacionales
The rebels' own name for their side; 'Nationalists' in English.
Rojos
'Reds' — period Nationalist term for all supporters of the Republic; today it reads as partisan.
Bando
A side in the war (bando nacional, bando republicano); also a military proclamation, e.g. declaring a state of war.
Retirada
The mass flight of Republican soldiers and civilians from Catalonia into France in January–February 1939.
Desbandá
The flight of civilians from Málaga along the coast road to Almería in February 1937, attacked from sea and air.
Cinturón de Hierro
Bilbao's 'Iron Belt' — the fortified line around the city, breached in June 1937.
Blocao
A small blockhouse or fortified post, often concrete, used by both sides.
Nido de ametralladora
Machine-gun nest — a concrete or stone emplacement, common on static fronts.
Refugio
Air-raid shelter; hundreds were dug in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Cartagena and Almería.
SIM
Servicio de Investigación Militar — the Republic's military intelligence and counter-espionage service from 1937, with its own prisons.
Comisario
Political commissar in the Popular Army, responsible for morale and political education.
Maquis
Anti-Franco guerrillas who continued fighting in the mountains after 1939, into the late 1940s and beyond.
Valle de Cuelgamuros
The monumental basilica and cross near El Escorial built by Franco (Valle de los Caídos until 2022).
Ley de Memoria Democrática
Law 20/2022 on democratic memory, which replaced the 2007 Historical Memory Law.

battles.name: Battle for Madrid
battles.place: Casa de Campo and Ciudad Universitaria, western Madrid
battles.why: After relieving Toledo, Franco's Army of Africa columns under Varela (with Mola in overall command) attacked Madrid from the south-west, expecting the capital to fall quickly and end the war. The government left for Valencia on 6 November; General Miaja and Vicente Rojo organised the defence.
battles.rep: Madrid militias and new mixed brigades under Miaja and Rojo (Líster, Durruti Column), XI and XII International Brigades, Soviet T-26 tanks and fighters
battles.nat: Varela's columns of Legionaries and Moroccan Regulares (Asensio, Barrón, Castejón, Delgado Serrano, Tella, Yagüe), Italian tankettes, German and Italian aircraft
battles.result: Republican defensive success. The Nationalists crossed the Manzanares into the Ciudad Universitaria but were stopped; on 23 November Franco called off the frontal assault. The front froze here until March 1939.
battles.visit: Today: bunkers and trench remains in the Casa de Campo and Parque del Oeste, pockmarked buildings and memorial plaques in the Ciudad Universitaria (e.g. around the School of Architecture and the old Clinical Hospital).

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: Varela's columns attack through the Casa de Campo and Carabanchel towards the Manzanares bridges. Militias, with Soviet tanks and aircraft, hold on the river line; the XI International Brigade marches into the Casa de Campo.

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: Bitter fighting in the Casa de Campo woods; Garabitas hill falls to the Nationalists and becomes their artillery position. Carabanchel is contested street by street. The XII Brigade and the Durruti Column arrive.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: Asensio's column crosses the Manzanares by a footbridge and breaks into the Ciudad Universitaria, taking the School of Architecture and part of the Clinical Hospital. Room-by-room fighting follows; Durruti is mortally wounded on 19 November.

phases.name: Phase 4
phases.cap: Counter-attacks cannot dislodge the Nationalist wedge, and the attackers cannot go further. On 23 November Franco stops the frontal assault. Both sides dig in; the Ciudad Universitaria front is static until March 1939.

battles.name: Battle of Jarama
battles.place: Jarama valley between San Martín de la Vega, Morata de Tajuña and Arganda, south-east of Madrid
battles.why: Having failed to take Madrid head-on, Franco tried to cut the Madrid–Valencia road, the capital's lifeline, by crossing the Jarama river south-east of the city.
battles.rep: Republican Army of the Centre under Pozas and then Miaja, with Líster and El Campesino, the XI, XII, XIV and XV International Brigades (British Battalion, Lincoln Battalion), Soviet tanks and aircraft
battles.nat: Varela's forces: five brigades of Legionaries and Regulares (García Escámez, Asensio, Barrón, Sáenz de Buruaga, Rada), Condor Legion guns and aircraft
battles.result: Stalemate. The Nationalists crossed the river and held a bridgehead, but the Madrid–Valencia road stayed in Republican hands. Losses were heavy on both sides; estimates vary widely.
battles.visit: Today: the Museo Batalla del Jarama in Morata de Tajuña, preserved trenches and monuments around the Pingarrón and 'Suicide Hill' area, and the International Brigades memorial near the road to Chinchón; guided routes are run from Morata.

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: The Nationalists attack across the west bank, take the heights of La Marañosa and close up to the Jarama along its length.

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: Moroccan troops silently kill the International Brigade sentries at the Pindoque bridge; Nationalist brigades cross there and at San Martín and push onto the plateau. The British Battalion is shattered defending 'Suicide Hill'.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: Nationalist pushes towards Arganda and the Valencia road are stopped by Líster, El Campesino, the International Brigades and Soviet tanks and aircraft. Miaja takes unified command.

phases.name: Phase 4
phases.cap: Republican counter-attacks on the Pingarrón heights fail with heavy loss; the Lincoln Battalion attacks on 27 February almost without artillery support. The front settles into trenches.

battles.name: Battle of Guadalajara
battles.place: The Zaragoza–Madrid road (N-II) and the Tajuña valley around Trijueque, Torija and Brihuega
battles.why: Fresh from Málaga, Mussolini's CTV was to strike down the Zaragoza road towards Guadalajara and Alcalá de Henares, meeting a renewed push from Jarama and encircling Madrid from the north-east.
battles.rep: Republican IV Corps: Líster's 11th Division, Cipriano Mera's 14th Division, XI and XII International Brigades (incl. the Italian Garibaldi Battalion), Soviet T-26 tanks and aircraft from permanent airfields
battles.nat: Italian CTV under Roatta (divisions 'Dio lo vuole', Fiamme Nere, Penne Nere and Littorio) with the Spanish Soria Division (Moscardó)
battles.result: Republican victory. The Italians were halted and driven back about 20 km (Wikipedia gives some 17,400 Italian and Spanish casualties against 6,258 Republican; figures vary). A major propaganda defeat for Mussolini.
battles.visit: Today: the Palacio de Ibarra ruins near Brihuega, the walls and cemetery of Brihuega, bunkers and positions along the N-II near Trijueque and Torija; few interpretation panels.

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: Italian motorised columns break through the thin Republican front near Almadrones and advance down the highway in sleet; a second column takes Brihuega on 10 March.

items.l: Rain and mud ground the Italian aircraft

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: The advance is stopped in front of Torija. At the Palacio de Ibarra, Italian volunteers of the Garibaldi Battalion fight Italian fascist troops. Republican aircraft from concrete runways strafe the columns jammed on the road; Trijueque is retaken on 13 March.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: The Republican counter-offensive: Líster attacks up the highway while Mera's 14th Division crosses the Tajuña and outflanks Brihuega. The Italians abandon the town and retreat in disorder.

phases.name: Phase 4
phases.cap: The Republicans advance some kilometres until the front stabilises; the Italians are withdrawn to reorganise. Captured Italian prisoners and documents are shown to the world press.

battles.name: Belchite
battles.place: Belchite, Quinto and Codo, south-east of Zaragoza
battles.why: To relieve pressure on the collapsing northern front (Santander), the Republic launched an offensive on the Aragon front aimed at Zaragoza, attacking on a broad front south of the Ebro.
battles.rep: Army of the East under Pozas, planned by Rojo: Walter's 35th Division (XI and XV International Brigades), Líster's 11th Division, Kléber's 45th Division, Soviet tanks and aircraft
battles.nat: V Army Corps (Ponte); the Belchite garrison of soldiers, Falangists and Requetés (commonly given as up to about 5,000 incl. militia), with a relief force under Barrón and Sáenz de Buruaga
battles.result: Tactical Republican success, strategic failure: Quinto, Codo and Belchite were taken, but Zaragoza was not reached and the northern campaign was not halted. Wikipedia lists about 2,000 Nationalist dead and 2,411 prisoners at Belchite, and heavy Republican losses; figures vary.
battles.visit: Today: the ruined Pueblo Viejo of Belchite, left as a war memorial (guided visits only), the ruined churches of San Martín and San Agustín; trench remains around Codo and Quinto.

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: Republican divisions attack along a wide front without preliminary bombardment. Quinto falls on 26 August after fighting for the church and Purburell hill; Codo is taken on 25 August, its Requetés largely killed or captured.

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: Belchite is encircled. A Nationalist relief force pushes from Zaragoza towards Mediana and gets within a few kilometres but is held; the Republicans fail to exploit towards Zaragoza.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: House-to-house fighting through the old town, the San Agustín church and the seminary under heat, thirst and bombardment. The last defenders try to break out on the night of 5–6 September; the town falls on 6 September.

phases.name: Aftermath
phases.cap: A last Republican tank attack at Fuentes de Ebro on 13 October fails. Belchite is retaken by the Nationalists on 10 March 1938. Franco later builds a new town beside the ruins and leaves the old one as a monument.

battles.name: Battle of Teruel
battles.place: Teruel and its surrounding heights — La Muela, El Muletón, Concud, the Alfambra valley
battles.why: Rojo launched a surprise attack on the exposed Nationalist salient of Teruel to pre-empt a new Nationalist offensive on Madrid and show the Popular Army could take a provincial capital.
battles.rep: Army of the Levant under Hernández Saravia: XVIII, XX and XXII Corps, Líster's 11th Division, El Campesino's 46th Division; International Brigades later
battles.nat: Teruel garrison under Colonel Rey d'Harcourt (a few thousand troops and civilians); relief and counter-offensive by Varela's Castile Corps and Aranda's Galicia Corps, Yagüe's Moroccan Corps, Condor Legion
battles.result: Nationalist victory. Teruel was captured by the Republicans on 8 January and retaken by the Nationalists on 22 February 1938 in bitter cold; Wikipedia estimates about 110,000 combined casualties including frostbite and sickness. The Popular Army's reserves were exhausted.
battles.visit: Today: Teruel's rebuilt old town and the ruined Seminary area, bunkers on La Muela and at Concud, and the Centro de Interpretación de la Batalla del Alfambra; a Civil War museum in Teruel is planned for 2028.

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: In deep snow and without preliminary bombardment, Republican columns close a ring around Teruel from north and south; Líster's division cuts the Zaragoza road at Concud. La Muela and El Mansueto are stormed and the garrison is pushed into the town.

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: Street fighting for the Seminary, the Bank of Spain and the Civil Government. A Nationalist relief under Varela and Aranda reaches La Muela on 31 December before a four-day blizzard (temperatures near −20°C) halts everything. Rey d'Harcourt surrenders on 8 January.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: The Nationalists switch their main effort north: in the Alfambra valley Yagüe's and Aranda's corps, led by a cavalry division in one of the last great cavalry charges, destroy the Republican front and take thousands of prisoners.

phases.name: Phase 4
phases.cap: Nationalist pincers close north and south of the town. Republican units withdraw down the Turia valley; on 22 February Teruel is back in Nationalist hands, a ruin. The way is open for the spring offensive to the sea.

battles.name: Battle of the Ebro
battles.place: The Ebro bend in the Terra Alta and Ribera d'Ebre: Riba-roja, Flix, Ascó, Móra d'Ebre, Miravet, Corbera, Gandesa, Serra de Pàndols and Serra de Cavalls
battles.why: With Valencia threatened after the Nationalist drive to the sea, Negrín and Rojo ordered a surprise crossing of the Ebro to reconnect the two halves of the Republic, relieve Valencia and show the world, before Munich, that the Republic could still fight.
battles.rep: Army of the Ebro under Modesto: Tagüeña's XV Corps (north), Líster's V Corps (centre), XII Corps; XI, XIII, XIV, XV International Brigades (withdrawn from late September)
battles.nat: Yagüe's Moroccan Corps initially holding the river, then Franco's reserves: García Valiño's Maestrazgo Corps and others, massed artillery, the Condor Legion and Italian aviation
battles.result: Nationalist victory. After advancing up to about 20 km the Republicans were stopped at Gandesa, then ground down over four months of counter-attacks. Casualty estimates range from 50,000 to over 100,000. The Army of the Ebro was destroyed, opening the way to Catalonia.
battles.visit: Today: the ruined Poble Vell of Corbera d'Ebre, the Memorial de les Camposines, the Serra de Pàndols memorial, trench and bunker sites at Punta Alta (Vilalba dels Arcs), Les Devees (Flix) and others, and interpretation centres coordinated by COMEBE.

phases.name: Phase 1
phases.cap: Shortly after midnight Republican assault troops cross in boats at a dozen points between Riba-roja and Miravet; engineers throw footbridges and pontoons across. Yagüe's thin defence is overrun; a diversion at Amposta fails with heavy loss for the XIV International Brigade.

phases.name: Phase 2
phases.cap: The Republicans reach the edge of Gandesa but cannot take it; the XV International Brigade fails repeatedly against Hill 481. Nationalist reinforcements arrive; aircraft bomb the bridges, and upstream dams are opened to flood the river.

phases.name: Phase 3
phases.cap: Successive Nationalist counter-offensives batter the bridgehead in summer heat on bare rocky ridges: Serra de Pàndols, Serra de Cavalls, Corbera. Artillery and bombing dominate; both sides suffer enormous losses. The International Brigades are withdrawn in late September.

phases.name: Phase 4
phases.cap: The decisive Nationalist attack breaks through at the Serra de Cavalls; the Republicans fall back to the river. The last Republican troops recross at Flix on 16 November. The Army of the Ebro is spent.
